There were the first Christian churches, where Christ had himself laid the foundation. <div eID="gen29365" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29366" type="x-p"/> 2. They made a good use of this lucid interval. Instead of growing more secure and wanton in the day of their prosperity, they abounded more in their duty, and made a good use of their tranquillity. (1.) They <hi type="italic">were edified,</hi> were built up in their most holy faith; the more free and constant enjoyment they had of the means of knowledge and grace, the more they increased in knowledge and grace. (2.) They <hi type="italic">walked in the fear of the Lord</hi>—were more exemplary themselves for a holy heavenly conversation. They so lived that all who conversed with them might say, Surely the fear of God reigns in those people. (3.) They <hi type="italic">walked in the comfort of the Holy Ghost</hi>—were not only faithful, but cheerful, in religion; they stuck to the ways of the Lord, and sang in those ways. <hi type="italic">The comfort of the Holy Ghost</hi> was their consolation, and that which they made their chief joy. They had recourse to the comfort of the Holy Ghost, and lived upon that, not only in days of trouble and affliction, but in days of rest and prosperity. The comforts of the earth, when they had the most free and full enjoyment of them, could not content them without the comfort of the Holy Ghost. Observe the connection of these two: when they walked <hi type="italic">in the fear of the Lord,</hi> then they walked <hi type="italic">in the comfort of the Holy Ghost.</hi> Those are most likely to walk cheerfully that walk circumspectly. <div eID="gen29366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29367" type="x-p"/> 3. God blessed it to them for their increase in number: They <hi type="italic">were multiplied.</hi> Sometimes the church multiplies the more for its being afflicted, as Israel in Egypt; yet if it were always so, the saints of the Most High would be worn out. At other times its rest contributes to its growth, as it enlarges the opportunity of ministers, and invites those in who at first are afraid of suffering. Or, <hi type="italic">then,</hi> when <hi type="italic">they walked in the fear of God and his comforts, they were multiplied.</hi> Thus those that will not be won by the word may be won by the conversation of professors.
entries.4d9ac184f8e952fd49d41645a5a51740f06b3b2e: <div eID="gen29367" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Cure of Æneas.</title> <div sID="gen29368" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">32</hi> And it came to pass, as Peter passed throughout all <hi type="italic">quarters,</hi> he came down also to the saints which dwelt at Lydda. <hi type="super">33</hi> And there he found a certain man named Æneas, which had kept his bed eight years, and was sick of the palsy. <hi type="super">34</hi> And Peter said unto him, Æneas, Jesus Christ maketh thee whole: arise, and make thy bed. And he arose immediately. <hi type="super">35</hi> And all that dwelt at Lydda and Saron saw him, and turned to the Lord. <div eID="gen29368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29369" type="x-p"/> Here we have, I. The visit Peter made to the churches that were newly planted by the dispersed preachers, <reference osisRef="Acts.9.32">v. 32</reference>. 1. He <hi type="italic">passed through all quarters.</hi> As an apostle, he was not to be the resident pastor of any one church, but the itinerant visitor of many churches, to confirm the doctrine of inferior preachers, to confer <hi type="italic">the Holy Ghost on those that believed,</hi> and to ordain ministers. He passed <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">dia panton</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">among them all,</hi> who pertained to the churches of Judea, Galilee, and Samaria, mentioned in the foregoing chapter. He was, like his Master, always upon the remove, and <hi type="italic">went about doing good;</hi> but still his head-quarters were at Jerusalem, for there we shall find him imprisoned, <reference osisRef="Acts.12.2">ch. xii. 2</reference>. <hi type="italic">He came to the saints at Lydda.</hi> This seems to be the same with <hi type="italic">Lod,</hi> a city in the tribe of Benjamin, mentioned <reference osisRef="1Chr.8.12">1 Chron. viii. 12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezra.2.33">Ezra ii. 33</reference>. The Christians are called <hi type="italic">saints,</hi> not only some particular eminent ones, as saint Peter and saint Paul, but every sincere professor of the faith of Christ. These are the saints on the earth, <reference osisRef="Ps.16.3">Ps. xvi. 3</reference>. <div eID="gen29369" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29370" type="x-p"/> II. The cure Peter wrought on <hi type="italic">Eneas,</hi> a man that had been bedridden eight years, <reference osisRef="Acts.9.33">v. 33</reference>. 1. His case was very deplorable: <hi type="italic">He was sick of the palsy,</hi> a dumb palsy, perhaps a dead palsy. The disease was extreme, for <hi type="italic">he kept his bed;</hi> it was inveterate, for he kept his bed <hi type="italic">eight years;</hi> and we may suppose that both he himself and all about him despaired of relief for him, and concluded upon no other than that he must still keep his bed till he removed to his grave. Christ chose such patients as this, whose disease was incurable in a course of nature, to show how desperate the case of fallen mankind was when he undertook their cure. When we were without strength, as this poor man, <hi type="italic">he sent his word to heal us.</hi> 2. His cure was very admirable, <reference osisRef="Acts.9.34">v. 34</reference>. (1.) Peter interested Christ in his case, and engaged him for his relief: <hi type="italic">Eneas, Jesus Christ maketh thee whole.</hi> Peter does not pretend to do it himself by any power of his own, but declares it to be Christ's act and deed, directs him to look up to Christ for help, and assures him of an <hi type="italic">immediate</hi> cure—not, "He <hi type="italic">will</hi> make thee," but, "He <hi type="italic">does</hi> make thee, whole;" and a <hi type="italic">perfect</hi> cure—not, "He makes thee <hi type="italic">easy,</hi>" but "He makes thee <hi type="italic">whole.</hi>" He does not express himself by way of prayer to Christ that he would make him whole, but as one having authority from Christ, and that knew his mind, he declares him made whole. (2.) He ordered him to bestir himself, to exert himself: "<hi type="italic">Arise and make thy bed,</hi> that all may see thou art thoroughly cured." Let none say that because it is Christ that by the power of his grace works all our works in us therefore we have no work, no duty, to do; for, though Jesus Christ makes thee whole, yet thou must arise and make use of the power he gives thee: "<hi type="italic">Arise, and make thy bed,</hi> to be to thee no longer a bed of sickness, but a bed of rest." (3.) Power went along with this word: he arose immediately, and no doubt very willingly made his own bed. <div eID="gen29370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29371" type="x-p"/> III. The good influence this had upon many (<reference osisRef="Acts.9.35">v. 35</reference>): <hi type="italic">All that dwelt at Lydda and Saron saw him, and turned to the Lord.</hi> We can scarcely think that every individual person in those countries took cognizance of the miracle, and was wrought upon by it; but many, the generality of the people in the town of Lydda and in the country of Saron, or Sharon, a fruitful plain or valley, of which it was foretold, <hi type="italic">Sharon shall be a fold of flocks,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.65.10">Isa. lxv. 10</reference>. 1. They all made enquiry into the truth of the miracle, did not overlook it, but saw him that was healed, and saw that it was a miraculous cure that was wrought upon him by the power of Christ, in his name, and with a design to confirm and ratify that doctrine of Christ which was now preached to the world. 2. They all submitted to the convincing proof and evidence there was in this of the divine origin of the Christian doctrine, and <hi type="italic">turned to the Lord,</hi> to the Lord Jesus. They turned from Judaism to Christianity; they embraced the doctrine of Christ, and submitted to his ordinances, and turned themselves over to him to be ruled and taught and saved by him.
entries.8ef437b63ca0125f32eb2d83977a121aff1ba7e5: <div eID="gen29371" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Tabitha Raised to Life.</title> <div sID="gen29372" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">36</hi> Now there was at Joppa a certain disciple named Tabitha, which by interpretation is called Dorcas: this woman was full of good works and almsdeeds which she did. <hi type="super">37</hi> And it came to pass in those days, that she was sick, and died: whom when they had washed, they laid <hi type="italic">her</hi> in an upper chamber. 38 And forasmuch as Lydda was nigh to Joppa, and the disciples had heard that Peter was there, they sent unto him two men, desiring <hi type="italic">him</hi> that he would not delay to come to them. 39 Then Peter arose and went with them. When he was come, they brought him into the upper chamber: and all the widows stood by him weeping, and showing the coats and garments which Dorcas made, while she was with them. <hi type="super">40</hi> But Peter put them all forth, and kneeled down, and prayed; and turning <hi type="italic">him</hi> to the body said, Tabitha, arise. And she opened her eyes: and when she saw Peter, she sat up. <hi type="super">41</hi> And he gave her <hi type="italic">his</hi> hand, and lifted her up, and when he had called the saints and widows, presented her alive. <hi type="super">42</hi> And it was known throughout all Joppa; and many believed in the Lord. <hi type="super">43</hi> And it came to pass, that he tarried many days in Joppa with one Simon a tanner. <div eID="gen29372" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29373" type="x-p"/> Here we have another miracle wrought by Peter, for the confirming of the gospel, and which exceeded the former—the raising of Tabitha to life when she had been for some time dead. Here is, <div eID="gen29373" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29374" type="x-p"/> I. The life, and death, and character of Tabitha, on whom this miracle was wrought, <reference osisRef="Acts.9.36-Acts.9.37">v. 36, 37</reference>. 1. She lived at Joppa, a sea-port town in the tribe of Dan, where Jonah took shipping to go to Tarshish, now called <hi type="italic">Japho.</hi> 2. Her name was <hi type="italic">Tabitha,</hi> a Hebrew name, the Greek for which is <hi type="italic">Dorcas,</hi> both signifying a <hi type="italic">doe,</hi> or <hi type="italic">hind,</hi> or <hi type="italic">deer,</hi> a pleasant creature. <hi type="italic">Naphtali</hi> is compared to <hi type="italic">a hind let loose, giving goodly words;</hi> and the wife to the kind and tender husband is as the loving <hi type="italic">hind,</hi> and as the pleasant <hi type="italic">roe,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.5.19">Prov. v. 19</reference>. 3. She was a disciple, one that had embraced the faith of Christ and was baptized; and not only so, but was eminent above many for works of charity. She showed her faith by her works, her good works, which she was full of, that is, in which she abounded. Her head was full of cares and contrivances which way she should do good. She <hi type="italic">devised liberal things,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.32.8">Isa. xxxii. 8</reference>. Her hands were full of good employment; she made a business of doing good, was never idle, having learned to <hi type="italic">maintain good works</hi> (<reference osisRef="Titus.3.8">Tit. iii. 8</reference>), to keep up a constant course and method of them. She was <hi type="italic">full of good works,</hi> as a tree that is full of fruit. Many are full of good words, who are empty and barren in good works; but Tabitha was a great doer, no great talker: <hi type="italic">Non magna loquimur, sed vivimus—We do not talk great things, but we live them.</hi> Among other good works, she was remarkable for her <hi type="italic">alms—deeds, which she did,</hi> not only her works of piety, which are good works and the fruits of faith, but works of charity and beneficence, flowing from love to her neighbour and a holy contempt of this world. Observe, She is commended not only for the alms which she gave, but for the alms—deeds which she did. Those that have not estates wherewith to give in charity may yet be able to do in charity, working with their hands, or walking with their feet, for the benefit of the poor. And those who will not do a charitable deed, whatever they may pretend, if they were rich would not bestow a charitable gift. She was full of alms—deeds, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">hon epoiei</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">which she made;</hi> there is an emphasis upon her <hi type="italic">doing</hi> them, because what her hand found to do of this kind she did with all her might, and persevered in. They were alms—deeds, not which she purposed and designed and said she would do, but which she did; not which she began to do, but which she did, which she went through with, which she performed the doing of, <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.11">2 Cor. viii. 11</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.9.7">ix. 7</reference>. This is the life and character of a certain disciple,; and should be of all the disciples of Christ; for, if we thus bear much fruit, then are we his disciples indeed, <reference osisRef="John.15.8">John xv. 8</reference>. 4. She was removed in the midst of her usefulness (<reference osisRef="Acts.9.37">v. 37</reference>): <hi type="italic">In those days she fell sick, and died.</hi> It is promised to those who consider the poor, not that they shall never be sick, but that the Lord will <hi type="italic">strengthen them upon the bed of languishing,</hi> at least with strength in their souls, and so will <hi type="italic">make all their bed in their sickness,</hi> will make it easy, <reference osisRef="Ps.41.1">Ps. xli. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.41.3">3</reference>. They cannot hope that they shall never die (<hi type="italic">merciful men are taken away,</hi> and merciful women too, witness Tabitha), but they may hope that they shall <hi type="italic">find mercy of the Lord in that day,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.18">2 Tim. i. 18</reference>. 5. Her friends and those about her did not presently bury her, as usual, because they were in hopes Peter would come and raise her to life again; but they <hi type="italic">washed the dead body,</hi> according to the custom, which, it is said, was with warm water, which, if there were any life remaining in the body, would recover it; so that this was done to show that she was really and truly dead. They tried all the usual methods to bring her to life, and could not. <hi type="italic">Conclamatum est—the last cry was uttered.</hi> They <hi type="italic">laid her out</hi> in her grave-clothes <hi type="italic">in an upper chamber,</hi> which Dr. Lightfoot thinks was probably the public meeting-room for the believers of that town; and they laid the body there, that Peter, if he would come, might raise her to life the more solemnly in that place. <div eID="gen29374" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29375" type="x-p"/> II. The request which her Christian friends sent to Peter to come to them with all speed, not to attend the funeral, but, if it might be, to prevent it, <reference osisRef="Acts.9.38">v. 38</reference>. Lydda, where Peter now was, was nigh to Joppa, and the disciples at Joppa had heard that Peter was there, and that he had raised Eneas from a bed of languishing; and therefore they <hi type="italic">sent him two men,</hi> to make the message the more solemn and respectful, <hi type="italic">desiring him that he would not delay to come to them;</hi> not telling him the occasion, lest he should modestly decline coming upon so great an errand as to raise the dead: if they can but get him to them, they will leave it to him. Their friend was dead, and it was too late to send for a physician, but not too late to send for Peter. <hi type="italic">Post mortem medicus—a physician after death,</hi> is an absurdity, but not <hi type="italic">Post mortem apostolus—an apostle after death.</hi> <div eID="gen29375" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29376" type="x-p"/> III. The posture in which he found the survivors, when he came to them (<reference osisRef="Acts.9.30">v. 30</reference>): <hi type="italic">Peter arose and went with them.</hi> Though they did not tell him what they wanted him for, yet he was willing to go along with them, believing it was upon some good account or other that he was sent for. Let not faithful ministers grudge to be at every body's beck, as far as they have ability, when the great apostle <hi type="italic">made himself the servant of all,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.19">1 Cor. ix. 19</reference>. He found the corpse laid in the upper chamber, and attended by widows, probably such as were in the communion of the church, poor widows; there they were, <div eID="gen29376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29377" type="x-p"/> 1. Commending the deceased—a good work, when there was that in them which was truly commendable, and worthy of imitation, and when it is done modestly and soberly, and without flattery of the survivors or any sinister intention, but purely for the glory of God and the exciting of others to that which is virtuous and praiseworthy. The commendation of Tabitha was like her own virtues, not in word, but in deed. Here were no encomiums of her in orations, nor poems inscribed to her memory; but <hi type="italic">the widows showed the coats and garments which she made</hi> for them, and bestowed upon them <hi type="italic">while she was with them.</hi> It was the comfort of Job, while he lived, that the loins of the poor blessed him, because they were warmed with the fleece of his sheep, <reference osisRef="Job.31.20">Job xxxi. 20</reference>. And here it was the credit of Tabitha, when she was dead, that the backs of the widows praised her for the garments which she made them. And those are certainly best praised <hi type="italic">whose own works praise them in the gates,</hi> whether the words of others do or no. It is much more honourable to clothe a company of decrepit widows with needful clothing for night and day, who will pray for their benefactors when they do not see them, than to clothe a company of lazy footmen with rich liveries, who perhaps behind their backs will curse those that clothe them (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.21">Eccl. vii. 21</reference>); and it is what all that are wise and good will take a greater pleasure in, for goodness is true greatness, and will pass better in the account shortly. Observe, (1.) Into what channel Tabitha turned much of her charity. Doubtless there were other instances of her alms—deeds which she did, but this was now produced; she did, as it should seem with her own hands, <hi type="italic">make coats and garments</hi> for poor widows, who perhaps with their own labour could make a shift to get their bread, but could not earn enough to buy clothes. And this is an excellent piece of charity, <hi type="italic">If thou seest the naked, that thou cover him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.58.7">Isa. lviii. 7</reference>), and not think it enough to say, <hi type="italic">Be ye warmed,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.2.15-Jas.2.16">James ii. 15, 16</reference>. (2.) What a grateful sense the poor had of her kindness: <hi type="italic">They showed the coats,</hi> not ashamed to own that they were indebted to her for the clothes on their backs. Those are horribly ungrateful indeed who have kindness shown them and will not make at least an acknowledgment of it, by showing the kindness that is done them, as these widows here did. Those who receive alms are not obliged so industriously to conceal it, as those are who give alms. When the poor reflect upon the rich as uncharitable and unmerciful, they ought to reflect upon themselves, and consider whether they are not unthankful and ungrateful. Their showing the coats and garments which Dorcas made tended to the praise not only of her charity, but of her industry, according to the character of the virtuous woman, that she <hi type="italic">lays her hands to the spindle,</hi> or at least to the needle, and then <hi type="italic">stretches out her hand to the poor,</hi> and <hi type="italic">reaches forth her hands to the needy,</hi> of what she has worked; and, when God and the poor have thus had their due, <hi type="italic">she makes herself coverings of tapestry</hi> and <hi type="italic">her</hi> own <hi type="italic">clothing is silk and purple,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.31.19-Prov.31.22">Prov. xxxi. 19-22</reference>. <div eID="gen29377" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29378" type="x-p"/> 2. They were here lamenting the loss of her: The widows stood by Peter, weeping. When the merciful are taken away, it should be laid to heart, especially by those to whom they have been in a particular manner merciful. They need not weep for her; she is taken from the evil to come, <hi type="italic">she rests from her labours and her works follow her,</hi> besides those she leaves behind her: but they weep for themselves and for their children, who will soon find the want of such a good woman, that has not left her fellow. Observe, They take notice of what good Dorcas did <hi type="italic">while she was with them,</hi> but now she is gone from them, and this is their grief. Those that are charitable will find that the <hi type="italic">poor they have always with them;</hi> but it is well if those that are poor find that they have always the charitable with them. We must make a good use of the lights that yet a little while are with us, because they will not be always with us, will not be long with us: and when they are gone we shall think what they did when they were with us. It should seem, the widows wept before Peter, as an inducement to him, if he could do any thing, to have compassion on them and help them, and restore one to them that used to have compassion on them. When charitable people are dead, there is no praying them to life again; but, when they are sick, this piece of gratitude is owing to them, to pray for their recovery, that, if it be the will of God, those may be spared to live who can ill be spared to die. <div eID="gen29378" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29379" type="x-p"/> IV. The manner in which she was raised to life. 1. Privately: She was laid in the upper room where they used to have their public meetings, and, it should seem, there was great crowding about the dead body, in expectation of what would be done; <hi type="italic">but Peter put them all forth,</hi> all the weeping widows, all but some few relations of the family, or perhaps the heads of the church, to join with him in prayer; as Christ did, <reference osisRef="Matt.9.25">Matt. ix. 25</reference>. Thus Peter declined every thing that looked like vainglory and ostentation; they came to see, but he did not come to be seen. He put them all forth, that he might with the more freedom pour out his soul before God in prayer upon this occasion, and not be disturbed with their noisy and clamorous lamentations. 2. By prayer. In his healing Eneas there was an implied prayer, but in this greater work he addressed himself to God by solemn prayer, as Christ when he raised Lazarus; but Christ's prayer was with the authority of a Son, who <hi type="italic">quickens whom he will;</hi> Peter's with the submission of a servant, who is under direction, and therefore he <hi type="italic">knelt down and prayed.</hi> 3. By the word, a quickening word, a word which is spirit and life: <hi type="italic">He turned to the body,</hi> which intimates that when he prayed he turned from it; lest the sight of it should discourage his faith, he looked another way, to teach us, like Abraham, <hi type="italic">against hope, to believe in hope,</hi> and overlook the difficulties that lie in the way, <hi type="italic">not considering the body as now dead,</hi> lest we should <hi type="italic">stagger at the promise,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.4.19-Rom.4.20">Rom. iv. 19, 20</reference>. But, when he had prayed, he <hi type="italic">turned to the body,</hi> and spoke in his Master's name, according to his example: "<hi type="italic">Tabitha, arise;</hi> return to life again." Power went along with this word, and she came to life, <hi type="italic">opened her eyes</hi> which death had closed. Thus, in the raising of dead souls to spiritual life, the first sign of life is the opening of the eyes of the mind, <reference osisRef="Acts.26.18">ch. xxvi. 18</reference>. When she saw Peter, she sat up, to show that she was really and truly alive; and (<reference osisRef="Acts.9.41">v. 41</reference>) <hi type="italic">he gave her his hand and lifted her up,</hi> not as if she laboured under any remaining weakness, but thus he would as it were welcome her to life again, and give her the right hand of fellowship among the living, from whom she had been cut off. And, <hi type="italic">lastly,</hi> he <hi type="italic">called the saints and widows,</hi> who were all in sorrow for her death, and <hi type="italic">presented her alive</hi> to them, to their great comfort, particularly of the widows, who laid her death much to heart (<reference osisRef="Acts.9.41">v. 41</reference>); to them he presented her, as Elijah (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.17.23">1 Kings xvii. 23</reference>), and Elisha (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.36">2 Kings iv. 36</reference>), and Christ (<reference osisRef="Luke.7.15">Luke vii. 15</reference>), presented the dead sons alive to their mothers. The greatest joy and satisfaction are expressed by life from the dead. <div eID="gen29379" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29380" type="x-p"/> V. The good effect of this miracle. 1. Many were by it convinced of the truth of the gospel, that is was from heaven, and not of men, and believed in the Lord, <reference osisRef="Acts.9.42">v. 42</reference>. The thing was <hi type="italic">known throughout all Joppa;</hi> it would be in every body's mouth quickly, and, it being a town of seafaring men, the notice of it would be the sooner carried thence to other countries, and though some never minded it many were wrought upon by it. This was the design of miracles, to confirm a divine revelation. 2. Peter was hereby induced to continue some time in this city, <reference osisRef="Acts.9.43">v. 43</reference>. Finding that a door of opportunity was opened for him there, he tarried there many days, till he was sent thence, and sent for thence upon business to another place. He tarried not in the house of Tabitha, though she was rich, lest he should seem to seek his own glory; but he took up his lodgings with one Simon a tanner, an ordinary tradesman, which is an instance of his condescension and humility: and hereby he has taught us not to <hi type="italic">mind high things, but to condescend to those of low estate,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.12.16">Rom. xii. 16</reference>. And, though Peter might seem to be buried in obscurity here in the house of a poor tanner by the sea-side, yet hence God fetched him to a noble piece of service, which is recorded in the next chapter; for <hi type="italic">those that humble themselves shall be exalted.</hi>  <chapter eID="Acts.9"/> <div eID="gen29380" type="x-p"/>

entries.dd635a485a881aa952753b60e58eb96f53bd88d0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15739"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 9</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Acts.9.1-Acts.9.25">Ac 9:1-25</reference>. Conversion of Saul, and Beginnings of His Ministry.</title> <div sID="gen30315" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15739"/><hi type="bold">1. Saul, yet breathing out threatenings and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord, &c.--</hi>The emphatic "yet" is intended to note the remarkable fact, that up to this moment his blind persecuting rage against the disciples of the Lord burned as fiercely as ever. (In the teeth of this, Neander and Olshausen picture him deeply impressed with Stephen's joyful faith, remembering passages of the Old Testament confirmatory of the Messiahship of Jesus, and experiencing such a violent struggle as would inwardly prepare the way for the designs of God towards him. Is not dislike, if not unconscious disbelief, of sudden conversion at the bottom of this?) The word "slaughter" here points to cruelties not yet recorded, but the particulars of which are supplied by himself nearly thirty years afterwards: "And I persecuted this way unto the death" (<reference osisRef="Acts.22.4">Ac 22:4</reference>); "and when they were put to death, I gave my voice [vote] against them. And I punished them oft in every synagogue, and compelled them to [did my utmost to make them] blaspheme; and being exceedingly mad against them, I persecuted them even unto strange [foreign] cities" (<reference osisRef="Acts.26.10">Ac 26:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.26.11">11</reference>). All this was before his present journey. <div eID="gen30315" type="x-p"/>
entries.1d1ad07220cac3e3e40fab33d0b16b903e791370: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15740"/><div sID="gen30316" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15740"/><hi type="bold">2. desired ... letters--</hi>of authorization.<div eID="gen30316" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30317" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to Damascus--</hi>the capital of Syria and the great highway between eastern and western Asia, about one hundred thirty miles northeast of Jerusalem; the most ancient city perhaps in the world, and lying in the center of a verdant and inexhaustible paradise. It abounded (as appears from Josephus, Wars of the Jews, 2.20,2) with Jews, and with Gentile proselytes to the Jewish faith. Thither the Gospel had penetrated; and Saul, flushed with past successes, undertakes to crush it out.<div eID="gen30317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30318" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that if he found any of this way, whether men or women--</hi>Thrice are women specified as objects of his cruelty, as an aggravated feature of it (<reference osisRef="Acts.8.3">Ac 8:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.22.4">22:4</reference>; and here). <div eID="gen30318" type="x-p"/>
entries.5fcd629d7780039fe359d490424dede985e7a156: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15741"/><div sID="gen30319" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15741"/><hi type="bold">3. he came near Damascus--</hi>so <reference osisRef="Acts.22.6">Ac 22:6</reference>. Tradition points to a bridge near the city as the spot referred to. Events which are the turning points in one's history so imprint themselves upon the memory that circumstances the most trifling in themselves acquire by connection with them something of their importance, and are recalled with inexpressible interest.<div eID="gen30319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30320" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">suddenly--</hi>At what time of day, it is not said; for artless simplicity reigns here. But he himself emphatically states, in one of his narratives, that it was "about noon" (<reference osisRef="Acts.22.6">Ac 22:6</reference>), and in the other, "at midday" (<reference osisRef="Acts.26.13">Ac 26:13</reference>), when there could be no deception.<div eID="gen30320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30321" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">there shined round about him a light from heaven--</hi>"a great light (he himself says) above the brightness of the sun," then shining in its full strength. <div eID="gen30321" type="x-p"/>
entries.1e52794355975f2fb915fb30bc43bd4f586d09ba: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15742"/><div sID="gen30322" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15742"/><hi type="bold">4-6. he fell to the earth--</hi>and his companions with him (<reference osisRef="Acts.26.14">Ac 26:14</reference>), who "saw the light" (<reference osisRef="Acts.22.9">Ac 22:9</reference>).<div eID="gen30322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30323" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and heard a voice saying unto him--</hi>"in the Hebrew tongue" (<reference osisRef="Acts.26.14">Ac 26:14</reference>).<div eID="gen30323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30324" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Saul, Saul--</hi>a reduplication full of tenderness [De Wette]. Though his name was soon changed into "Paul," we find him, in both his own narratives of the scene, after the lapse of so many years, retaining the original form, as not daring to alter, in the smallest detail, the overpowering words addressed to him.<div eID="gen30324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30325" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">why persecutest thou me?--</hi>No language can express the affecting character of this question, addressed from the right hand of the Majesty on high to an infuriated, persecuting mortal. (See <reference osisRef="Matt.25.45">Mt 25:45</reference>, and that whole judgment scene). <div eID="gen30325" type="x-p"/>
entries.aacdbb73b220b44d2e1ffb2c4ae9681b7e09742f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15745"/><div sID="gen30331" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15745"/><hi type="bold">7. the men ... stood speechless--</hi>This may mean merely that they remained so; but if the standing posture be intended, we have only to suppose that though at first they "all fell to the earth" (<reference osisRef="Acts.26.14">Ac 26:14</reference>), they arose of their own accord while Saul yet lay prostrate.<div eID="gen30331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30332" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hearing a--</hi>rather "the"<div eID="gen30332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30333" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">voice--</hi>Paul himself says, "they heard not the voice of Him that spake to me" (<reference osisRef="Acts.22.9">Ac 22:9</reference>). But just as "the people that stood by heard" the voice that saluted our Lord with recorded words of consolation and assurance, and yet heard not the articulate words, but thought "it thundered" or that some "angel spake to Him" (<reference osisRef="John.12.28">Joh 12:28</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.12.29">29</reference>)--so these men heard the voice that spake to Saul, but heard not the articulate words. Apparent discrepancies like these, in the different narratives of the same scene in one and the same book of Acts, furnish the strongest confirmation both of the facts themselves and of the book which records them. <div eID="gen30333" type="x-p"/>
entries.1e35452fa7faf7815af7a7aac57d9f6a905dd559: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15746"/><div sID="gen30334" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15746"/><hi type="bold">8. Saul arose ... and when his eyes were opened, he saw no man--</hi>after beholding the Lord, since he "could not see for the glory of that light" (<reference osisRef="Acts.22.11">Ac 22:11</reference>), he had involuntarily closed his eyes to protect them from the glare; and on opening them again he found his vision gone. "It is not said, however, that he was blind, for it was no punishment" [Bengel]. <div eID="gen30334" type="x-p"/>
entries.c3c441da9991e6cd7defe8ced63afc8f66553ade: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15747"/><div sID="gen30335" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15747"/><hi type="bold">9. And he was three days without sight, and neither did eat nor drink--</hi>that is, according to the Hebrew mode of computation: he took no food during the remainder of that day, the entire day following, and so much of the subsequent day as elapsed before the visit of Ananias. Such a period of entire abstinence from food, in that state of mental absorption and revolution into which he had been so suddenly thrown, is in perfect harmony with known laws and numerous facts. But what three days those must have been! "Only one other space of three days' <hi type="bold">duration can be mentioned of equal importance in the history of the world" [Howson]. Since Jesus had been revealed not only to his eyes but to his soul (see on <reference osisRef="Gal.1.15">Ga 1:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.16">16</reference>), the double conviction must have immediately flashed upon him, that his whole reading of the Old Testament hitherto had been wrong, and that the system of legal righteousness in which he had, up to that moment, rested and prided himself was false and fatal. What materials these for spiritual exercise during those three days of total darkness, fasting, and solitude! On the one hand, what self-condemnation, what anguish, what death of legal hope, what difficulty in believing that in such a case there could be hope at all; on the other hand, what heartbreaking admiration of the grace that had "pulled him out of the fire," what resistless conviction that there must be a purpose of love in it, and what tender expectation of being yet honored, as a chosen vessel, to declare what the Lord had done for his soul, and to spread abroad the savor of that Name which he had so wickedly, though ignorantly, sought to destroy--</hi>must have struggled in his breast during those memorable days! Is it too much to say that all that profound insight into the Old Testament, that comprehensive grasp of the principles of the divine economy, that penetrating spirituality, that vivid apprehension of man's lost state, and those glowing views of the perfection and glory of the divine remedy, that beautiful ideal of the loftiness and the lowliness of the Christian character, that large philanthropy and burning zeal to spend and be spent through all his future life for Christ, which distinguish the writings of this chiefest of the apostles and greatest of men, were all quickened into life during those three successive days? <div eID="gen30335" type="x-p"/>
entries.2dfda19d72b22aadded40fa46f9c575e31074a3a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15748"/><div sID="gen30336" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15748"/><hi type="bold">10-16. a certain disciple ... named Ananias--</hi>See on <reference osisRef="Acts.22.12">Ac 22:12</reference>.<div eID="gen30336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30337" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to him said the Lord--</hi>that is, Jesus. (See <reference osisRef="Acts.9.13">Ac 9:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.14.17">14, 17</reference>). <div eID="gen30337" type="x-p"/>
entries.45738e689d84bd13f3dbaee82b3fd4d7d177efa5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15755"/><div sID="gen30349" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15755"/><hi type="bold">17-19. Ananias went his way, and putting his hands on him, said, Brother Saul--</hi>How beautifully childlike is the obedience of Ananias to "the heavenly vision!"<div eID="gen30349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30350" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the Lord, even Jesus--</hi>This clearly shows in what sense the term "Lord" is used in this book. It is Jesus that is meant, as almost invariably in the Epistles also.<div eID="gen30350" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30351" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">who appeared unto thee in the way--</hi>This knowledge by an inhabitant of Damascus of what had happened to Saul before entering it, would show him at once that this was the man whom Jesus had already prepared him to expect.<div eID="gen30351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30352" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and be filled with the Holy Ghost--</hi>which Ananias probably, without any express instructions on that subject, took it for granted would descend upon him; and not necessarily after his baptism [Baumgarten, Webster and Wilkinson]--for Cornelius and his company received it before theirs (<reference osisRef="Acts.10.44-Acts.10.48">Ac 10:44-48</reference>)--but perhaps immediately after the recovery of his sight by the laying on of Ananias' hands. <div eID="gen30352" type="x-p"/>
entries.ecdf82cef9b39f3efd91fa5e14c30e0e2624fd55: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15758"/><div sID="gen30357" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15758"/><hi type="bold">20-22. preached Christ ... that he is the Son of God--</hi>rather, "preached Jesus," according to all the most ancient manuscripts and versions of the New Testament (so <reference osisRef="Acts.9.21">Ac 9:21</reference>, "all that call on this name," that is, Jesus; and <reference osisRef="Acts.9.22">Ac 9:22</reference>, "proving that this Jesus is very Christ"). <div eID="gen30357" type="x-p"/>
entries.9b4f7233a5c04fd0ba8b5ceaa93d2ee6bef364ff: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15759"/><div sID="gen30358" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15759"/><hi type="bold">23. And after many days were fulfilled, the Jews took counsel to kill him--</hi>Had we no other record than this, we should have supposed that what is here related took place while Saul continued at Damascus after his baptism. But in <reference osisRef="Gal.1.17">Ga 1:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.18">18</reference> we learn from Paul himself that he "went into Arabia, and returned again unto Damascus," and that from the time of his first visit to the close of his second, both of which appear to have been short, a period of three years elapsed; either three full years, or one full year and part of two others. (See on <reference osisRef="Gal.1.16-Gal.1.18">Ga 1:16-18</reference>). That such a blank should occur in the Acts, and be filled up in Galatians, is not more remarkable than that the flight of the Holy Family into Egypt, their stay there, and their return thence, recorded only by Matthew, should be so entirely passed over by Luke, that if we had only his Gospel, we should have supposed that they returned to Nazareth immediately after the presentation in the temple. (Indeed in one of his narratives, <reference osisRef="Acts.22.16">Ac 22:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.22.17">17</reference>, Paul himself takes no notice of this period). But wherefore this journey? Perhaps (1) because he felt a period of repose and partial seclusion to be needful to his spirit, after the violence of the change and the excitement of his new occupation. (2) To prevent the rising storm which was gathering against him from coming too soon to a head. (3) To exercise his ministry in the Jewish synagogues, as opportunity afforded. On his return, refreshed and strengthened in spirit, he immediately resumed his ministry, but soon to the imminent hazard of his life. <div eID="gen30358" type="x-p"/>
entries.6f3fddbfa88e9a35e79401bee075c16697a20dd0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15760"/><div sID="gen30359" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15760"/><hi type="bold">24-25. they watched the gates night and day to kill him--</hi>The full extent of his danger appears only from his own account (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.32">2Co 11:32</reference>): "In Damascus, the governor under Aretas the king kept the city of the Damascenes with a garrison, desirous to apprehend me"; the exasperated Jews having obtained from the governor a military force, the more surely to compass his destruction. <div eID="gen30359" type="x-p"/>
entries.86bd9c98306ec4817b6fca9d20ae1ffb1110fed9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15762"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Acts.9.26-Acts.9.31">Ac 9:26-31</reference>. Saul's First Visit to Jerusalem after His Conversion.</title> <div sID="gen30362" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15762"/><hi type="bold">26. And when Saul was come to Jerusalem--</hi>"three years after" his conversion, and particularly "to see Peter" (<reference osisRef="Gal.1.18">Ga 1:18</reference>); no doubt because he was the leading apostle, and to communicate to him the prescribed sphere of his labors, specially to "the Gentiles."<div eID="gen30362" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30363" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he assayed to join himself to the disciples--</hi>simply as one of them, leaving his apostolic commission to manifest itself.<div eID="gen30363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30364" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they were all afraid of him, &c.--</hi>knowing him only as a persecutor of the faith; the rumor of his conversion, if it ever was cordially believed, passing away during his long absence in Arabia, and the news of his subsequent labors in Damascus perhaps not having reached them. <div eID="gen30364" type="x-p"/>
entries.a6d3de46ff42d1817e7096c48c42317c91d1d9e2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15763"/><div sID="gen30365" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15763"/><hi type="bold">27. But Barnabas ... brought him to the apostles--</hi>that is, to Peter and James; for "other of the apostles saw I none," says he fourteen years after (<reference osisRef="Gal.1.18">Ga 1:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.19">19</reference>). Probably none of the other apostles were there at the time (<reference osisRef="Acts.4.36">Ac 4:36</reference>). Barnabas being of Cyprus, which was within a few hours' sail of Cilicia, and annexed to it as a Roman province, and Saul and he being Hellenistic Jews and eminent in their respective localities, they may very well have been acquainted with each other before this [Howson]. What is here said of Barnabas is in fine consistency with the "goodness" ascribed to him (<reference osisRef="Acts.11.24">Ac 11:24</reference>), and with the name "son of consolation," given him by the apostles (<reference osisRef="Acts.4.36">Ac 4:36</reference>); and after Peter and James were satisfied, the disciples generally would at once receive him.<div eID="gen30365" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30366" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">how he had seen the Lord ... and he--</hi>the Lord.<div eID="gen30366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30367" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">had spoken to him--</hi>that is, how he had received his commission direct from the Lord Himself. <div eID="gen30367" type="x-p"/>
entries.3d0e80a107bc7915b7346a07537338e8e9a92c2d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15764"/><div sID="gen30368" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15764"/><hi type="bold">28-29. And he was with them, coming in and going out at Jerusalem--</hi>for fifteen days, lodging with Peter (<reference osisRef="Gal.1.18">Ga 1:18</reference>). <div eID="gen30368" type="x-p"/>
entries.4c38b67a073482a562f2865b6751178e87d6583d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15766"/><div sID="gen30371" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15766"/><hi type="bold">30. they brought him down to Cæsarea--</hi>on the coast (see on <reference osisRef="Acts.8.40">Ac 8:40</reference>); accompanying him thus far. But Paul had another reason than his own apprehension for quitting Jerusalem so soon. "While he was praying in the temple, he was in a trance," and received express injunctions to this effect. (See on <reference osisRef="Acts.22.17-Acts.22.21">Ac 22:17-21</reference>).<div eID="gen30371" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30372" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and sent him forth to Tarsus--</hi>In <reference osisRef="Gal.1.21">Ga 1:21</reference> he himself says of this journey, that he "came into the regions of Syria and Cilicia"; from which it is natural to infer that instead of sailing direct for Tarsus, he landed at Seleucia, travelled thence to Antioch, and penetrated from this northward into Cilicia, ending his journey at Tarsus. As this was his first visit to his native city since his conversion, so it is not certain that he ever was there again. (See on <reference osisRef="Acts.11.25">Ac 11:25</reference>). It probably was now that he became the instrument of gathering into the fold of Christ those "kinsmen," that "sister," and perhaps her "son," of whom mention is made in <reference osisRef="Acts.23.16">Ac 23:16</reference>, &c.; <reference osisRef="Rom.16.7">Ro 16:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.21">11, 21</reference> [Howson]. <div eID="gen30372" type="x-p"/>
entries.57362395f69103a378bcf25083bc13b88baaf6a3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15767"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Acts.9.31">Ac 9:31</reference>. Flourishing State of the Church in Palestine at This Time.</title> <div sID="gen30373" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15767"/><hi type="bold">31. Then had all the churches rest--</hi>rather, "the Church," according to the best manuscripts and versions. But this rest was owing not so much to the conversion of Saul, as probably to the Jews being engrossed with the emperor Caligula's attempt to have his own image set up in the temple of Jerusalem [Josephus, Antiquities, 18.8.1, &c.].<div eID="gen30373" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30374" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">throughout all Judea, and Galilee, and Samaria--</hi>This incidental notice of distinct churches already dotting all the regions which were the chief scenes of our Lord's ministry, and that were best able to test the facts on which the whole preaching of the apostles was based, is extremely interesting. "The fear of the Lord" expresses their holy walk; "the comfort of the Holy Ghost," their "peace and joy in believing," under the silent operation of the blessed Comforter.<div eID="gen30374" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Acts.9.32-Acts.9.43">Ac 9:32-43</reference>. Peter Heals Eneas at Lydda and Raises Tabitha to Life at Joppa.</title> <div sID="gen30375" type="x-p"/> The historian now returns to Peter, in order to introduce the all-important narrative of Cornelius (<reference osisRef="Acts.10.1-Acts.10.48">Ac 10:1-48</reference>). The occurrences here related probably took place during Saul's sojourn in Arabia. <div eID="gen30375" type="x-p"/>
entries.e5da391708e5933f3caf176e556591f794126fb3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15768"/><div sID="gen30376" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15768"/><hi type="bold">32-35. as Peter passed throughout all quarters--</hi>not now fleeing from persecution, but peacefully visiting the churches.<div eID="gen30376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30377" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to the saints which dwelt at Lydda--</hi>about five miles east of Joppa. <div eID="gen30377" type="x-p"/>
entries.bb9bc7fb40a02c13dc9f0ab7ed7f7979818a38cc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15771"/><div sID="gen30382" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15771"/><hi type="bold">36-39. at Joppa--</hi>the modern Jaffa, on the Mediterranean, a very ancient city of the Philistines, afterwards and still the seaport of Jerusalem, from which it lies distant forty-five miles to the northwest.<div eID="gen30382" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30383" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Tabitha ... Dorcas--</hi>the Syro-Chaldaic and Greek names for an antelope or gazelle, which, from its loveliness, was frequently employed as a proper name for women [Meyer, Olshausen]. Doubtless the interpretation, as here given, is but an echo of the remarks made by the Christians regarding her--how well her character answered to her name.<div eID="gen30383" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30384" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">full of good works and alms-deeds--</hi>eminent for the activities and generosities of the Christian character. <div eID="gen30384" type="x-p"/>
entries.df7524587428298e5ad8a700a678d85a4651e8ba: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15775"/><div sID="gen30391" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15775"/><hi type="bold">40-43. Peter put them all forth, and kneeled down--</hi>the one in imitation of his Master's way (<reference osisRef="Luke.8.54">Lu 8:54</reference>; and compare <reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.33">2Ki 4:33</reference>); the other, in striking contrast with it. The kneeling became the lowly servant, but not the Lord Himself, of whom it is never once recorded that he knelt in the performance of a miracle.<div eID="gen30391" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30392" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">opened her eyes, and when she saw Peter, she sat up--</hi>The graphic minuteness of detail here imparts to the narrative an air of charming reality. <div eID="gen30392" type="x-p"/>

entries.ba7aa93100c2ba4e29b44579b300afa1fc0134e5: <div eID="gen43980" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen43981" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen43982" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen43982" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen43981" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen43983" type="x-p"/> Saul, bent on the destruction of the Christians, obtains letters from the high priest, authorizing him to seize those whom he should find at Damascus, and bring them bound to Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Act.9.1">Act 9:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Act.9.2">Act 9:2</reference>. On his way to Damascus, he has a Divine vision, is convinced of his sin and folly, is struck blind, and remains three days without sight, and neither eats nor drinks, <reference osisRef="Act.9.3-Act.9.9">Act 9:3-9</reference>. Ananias, a disciple, is commanded in a vision to go and speak to Saul, and restore his sight, <reference osisRef="Act.9.10-Act.9.16">Act 9:10-16</reference>. Ananias goes and lays his hands on him, and he receives his sight, and is baptized, <reference osisRef="Act.9.17-Act.9.19">Act 9:17-19</reference>. Saul, having spent a few days with the Christians at Damascus, goes to the synagogues, proclaims Christ, and confounds the Jews, <reference osisRef="Act.9.20-Act.9.22">Act 9:20-22</reference>. The Jews lay wait to kill him, but the disciples let him down over the walls of the city in a basket, by night, and he escapes to Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Act.9.23-Act.9.25">Act 9:23-25</reference>. Having wished to associate with the disciples there, they avoid him; but Barnabas takes and brings him to the apostles, and declares his conversion, <reference osisRef="Act.9.26">Act 9:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Act.9.27">Act 9:27</reference>. He continues in Jerusalem preaching Christ, and arguing with the Hellenistic Jews, who endeavor to slay him; but the disciples take him to Caesarea, and send him thence to his own city Tarsus, <reference osisRef="Act.9.28-Act.9.30">Act 9:28-30</reference>. About this time, the Churches, being freed from persecution, are edified and multiplied, <reference osisRef="Act.9.31">Act 9:31</reference>. Peter heals Eneas at Lydda, who had been afflicted with the palsy eight years: in consequence of which miracle, all the people of Lydda and Saron are converted, <reference osisRef="Act.9.32-Act.9.35">Act 9:32-35</reference>. Account of the sickness and death of a Christian woman named Tabitha, who dwelt at Joppa; and her miraculous restoration to life by the ministry of Peter, <reference osisRef="Act.9.36-Act.9.41">Act 9:36-41</reference>. Gracious effects produced among the inhabitants of Lydda by this miracle, <reference osisRef="Act.9.42">Act 9:42</reference>, <reference osisRef="Act.9.43">Act 9:43</reference>. <div eID="gen43983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43984" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen43984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43985" type="x-p"/> Saul, yet breathing out threatenings and slaughter - The original text is very emphatic, ετι εμπνεων απειλης και φονου, and points out how determinate Saul was to pursue and accomplish his fell purpose of totally destroying the infant Church of Christ. The mode of speech introduced above is very frequent in the Greek writers, who often express any vehement and hostile affection of the mind by the verb πνεειν, to breathe, to pant; so Theocritus, Idyll. xxii. ver. 82: Ες μεσσον συναγον, φονον αλλαλοισι πνεοντες. <div eID="gen43985" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43986" type="x-p"/> They came into the assembly, breathing mutual slaughter. <div eID="gen43986" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43987" type="x-p"/> Euripides has the same form, πυρ πνεουσα και φονον, breathing out fire, and slaughter, Iphig. in Taur. <div eID="gen43987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43988" type="x-p"/> And Aristophanes more fully, referring to all the preparations for war: - Αλλα πνεοντας δορυ και λογχας και λευκολοφους τρυφαλειας, Και πηληκας, και κνημιδας, και θυμους ἑπταβοειους. <div eID="gen43988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43989" type="x-p"/> They breathed spears, and pikes, and helmets, and crests, and greaves, and the fury of redoubted heroes. <div eID="gen43989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43990" type="x-p"/> The figure is a favourite one with Homer: hence μενεα πνειοντες Αβαντες, the Abantes breathing strength. - Il. ii. 536. And how frequently he speaks of his fierce countrymen as, μενεα πνειοντες Αχαιοι, the Greeks breathing strength, see Il. iii. 8; xi. 508; xxiv. 364, which phrase an old Scholiast interprets, being filled with strength and fury. St. Luke, who was master of the Greek tongue, chose such terms as best expressed a heart desperately and incessantly bent on accomplishing the destruction of the objects of its resentment. Such at this time was the heart of Saul of Tarsus; and it had already given full proof of its malignity, not only in the martyrdom of Stephen, but also in making havoc of the Church, and in forcibly entering every house, and dragging men and women, whom he suspected of Christianity, and committing them to prison. See <reference osisRef="Act.8.3">Act 8:3</reference>. <div eID="gen43990" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43991" type="x-p"/> Went unto the high priest - As the high priest was chief in all matters of an ecclesiastical nature, and the present business was pretendedly religious, he was the proper person to apply to for letters by which this virulent persecutor might be accredited. The letters must necessarily be granted in the name of the whole Sanhedrin, of which Gamaliel, Saul's master, was at that time the head; but the high priest was the proper organ through whom this business might be negotiated.
entries.22ddba42ccf31021469b004291363b0f64ce51ae: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen43991" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43992" type="x-p"/> Letters to Damascus to the synagogues - Damascus, anciently called דמסק Damask, and דרמסק Darmask, was once the metropolis of all Syria. It was situated at fifty miles' distance from the sea; from which it is separated by lofty mountains. It is washed by two rivers, Amara or Abara, which ran through it, and Pharpar, called by the Greeks Chrysorrhoas, the golden stream, which ran on the outside of its walls. It is one of the most ancient cities in the world, for it existed in the time of Abraham, <reference osisRef="Gen.14.15">Gen 14:15</reference>; and how long before is not known. The city of Damascus is at present a place of considerable trade, owing to its being the rendezvous for all the pilgrims from the north of Asia, on their road to and from the temple of Mecca. It is surrounded with pretty strong walls, which have nine gates, and is between four and five miles in circumference. It contains about 100,000 inhabitants, some say more, the principal part of whom are Arabs and Turks, with whom live, in a state of considerable degradation, about 15,000 Christians. Damascus, like other places of importance, has passed through the hands of many masters. It was captured and ruined by Tiglath Pileser, who carried away its inhabitants to Kin, beyond the Euphrates, about 740 years before the Christian era; and thus was fulfilled the prophecy of Isaiah, <reference osisRef="Isa.17.1-Isa.17.3">Isa 17:1-3</reference>, and that of Amos, <reference osisRef="Amo.1.4">Amo 1:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amo.1.5">Amo 1:5</reference>. It was also taken by Sennacherib, and by the generals of Alexander the Great. Metellus and Laelius seized it, during the war of Pompey with Tigranes; before Christ 65. It continued under the dominion of the Romans till the Saracens took possession of it, in a.d. 634. It was besieged and taken by Teemour lenk, a.d. 1400, who put all the inhabitants to the sword. The Egyptian Mamelukes repaired Damascus when they took possession of Syria; but the Turkish Emperor Selim having defeated them at the battle of Aleppo in 1516, Damascus was brought under the government of the Turks, and in their hands it still remains. In the time of St. Paul it was governed by Aretas, whose father, Obodas, had been governor of it under Augustus. Damascus is 112 miles south of Antioch; 130 N.N.E. of Jerusalem; and 270 S.S.W; of Diarbek. Longitude 37 east: latitude 33 45' north. The fruit tree called the Damascene, vulgarly Damazon, and the flower called the Damask rose, were transplanted from Damascus to the gardens of Europe; and the silks and linens, known by the name of Damasks, were probably first manufactured by the inhabitants of this ancient city. <div eID="gen43992" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43993" type="x-p"/> Any of this way - That is, this religion, for so דרך derec in Hebrew, and ὁδος, hodos, in Hellenistic Greek, are often to be understood. דרך יהוה derec Yehovah, the way of the Lord, implies the whole of the worship due to him, and prescribed by himself: the way or path in which he wills men to walk, that they may get safely through life, and finally attain everlasting felicity. The Jewish writers designate the whole doctrine and practice of Christianity by a similar expression, דרך הנוצרים derec hanotsarim, the way, doctrine, or sect of the Christians. <div eID="gen43993" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43994" type="x-p"/> Whether they were men or women - Provided they were Jews; for no converts had as yet been made among the Gentiles; nor did the power of the high priest and Sanhedrin extend to any but those who belonged to the synagogues. Pearce. <div eID="gen43994" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43995" type="x-p"/> In every country where there were Jews and synagogues, the power and authority of the Sanhedrin and high priest were acknowledged: just as papists in all countries acknowledge the authority of the pope. And as there can be but one pope, and one conclave, so there could be but one high priest, and one Sanhedrin; and this is the reason why the high priest and sanhedrin at Jerusalem had authority over all Jews, even in the most distant countries.
entries.34aff733579ee0e01f264971be77d8469cf0b5fd: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen43995" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43996" type="x-p"/> Suddenly there shined round about him - This might have been an extraordinary flash of the electric fluid, accompanied with thunder, with which God chose to astonish and confound Saul and his company; but so modified it as to prevent it from striking them dead. Thunder would naturally follow such a large quantity of this fluid as appears to have been disengaged at this time; and out of this thunder, or immediately after it, Christ spoke in an awful and distinct voice, which appears to have been understood by Saul only.
entries.14d9db96aabbb0aededb98e23d74b50dd80f1070: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen43996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43997" type="x-p"/> And he fell to the earth - Being struck down with the lightning: many persons suppose he was on horseback, and painters thus represent him; but this is utterly without foundation. Painters are, in almost every case, wretched commentators.
entries.1562da57ccd30d216bd1938baf38e4604682a965: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen43997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43998" type="x-p"/> Who art thou, Lord? - Τις ει, Κυριε; Who art thou, Sir? He had no knowledge who it was that addressed him, and would only use the term Κυριε, as any Roman or Greek would, merely as a term of civil respect. <div eID="gen43998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43999" type="x-p"/> I am Jesus whom thou persecutest - "Thy enmity is against me and my religion; and the injuries which thou dost to my followers I consider as done to myself." The following words, making twenty in the original, and thirty in our version, are found in no Greek MS. The words are, It is hard for thee to kick against the pricks: and he trembling and astonished said, Lord, what wilt thou have me to do? and the Lord said unto him. It is not very easy to account for such a large addition, which is not only not found in any Greek MS. yet discovered, but is wanting in the Itala, Erpen's Arabic, the Syriac, Coptic, Sahidic, and most of the Slavonian. It is found in the Vulgate, one of the Arabic, the Ethiopic, and Armenian; and was probably borrowed from <reference osisRef="Act.26.14">Act 26:14</reference>, and some marginal notes. It is wanting also in the Complutensian edition, and in that of Bengel. Griesbach also leaves it out of the text. <div eID="gen43999" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44000" type="x-p"/> It is hard for thee, etc. - Σκληρον σοι προς κεντρα λακτιζειν. This is a proverbial expression, which exists, not only in substance, but even in so many words, both in the Greek and Latin writers. Κεντρον, kentron, signifies an ox goad, a piece of pointed iron stuck in the end of a stick, with which the ox is urged on when drawing the plough. The origin of the proverb seems to have been this: sometimes it happens that a restive or stubborn ox kicks back against the goad, and thus wounds himself more deeply: hence it has become a proverb to signify the fruitlessness and absurdity of rebelling against lawful authority, and the getting into greater difficulties by endeavoring to avoid trifling sufferings. So the proverb, Incidit in Scyllam qui vult vitare Charybdim. Out of the cauldron into the fire. "Out of bad into worse." The saying exists, almost in the apostolic form, in the following writers. Euripides, in Bacch. ver. 793: - Θυοιμ' αν αυτῳ μαλλον, η θυμουμενος Προς κεντρα λακτιζοιμι, θνητος ων, Θεῳ. "I, who am a frail mortal, should rather sacrifice to him who is a God, than, by giving place to anger, kick against the goads." <div eID="gen44000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44001" type="x-p"/> And Aeschylus, in Agamemnon, ver. 1633: - Προς κεντρα μη λακτιζε. <div eID="gen44001" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44002" type="x-p"/> Kick not against the goads. <div eID="gen44002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44003" type="x-p"/> And again in Prometh. Vinct. ver. 323: - Προς κεντρα κωλον εκτενεις, ὁρων ὁτι Τραχυς μοναρχος ουδ' ὑπευθυνος κρατει. "Thou stretchest out thy foot against goads, seeing the fierce monarch governs according to his own will." <div eID="gen44003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44004" type="x-p"/> Resistance is of no use: the more thou dost rebel, the more keenly thou shalt suffer. See the Scholiast here. <div eID="gen44004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44005" type="x-p"/> Pindar has a similar expression, Pyth. ii. ver. 171-5: - Φερειν δ' ελαφρως Επαυχενιον λαβοντα Ζυγον γ' αρηγει. Ποτι κεντρον δε τοι Λακτιζεμεν, τελεθει Ολισθηρος οιμος. "It is profitable to bear willingly the assumed yoke. <div eID="gen44005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44006" type="x-p"/> To kick against the goad is pernicious conduct." <div eID="gen44006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44007" type="x-p"/> Where see the Scholiast, who shows that "it is ridiculous for a man to fight with fortune: for if the unruly ox, from whom the metaphor is taken, kick against the goad, he shall suffer still more grievously." Terence uses the same figure. Phorm. Act i. scen. 2, ver. 27: - <div eID="gen44007" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44008" type="x-p"/> Venere in mentem mihi istaec: nam inscitia est, <div eID="gen44008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44009" type="x-p"/> Adversum stimulum calces. - " <div eID="gen44009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44010" type="x-p"/> These things have come to my recollection, for it is foolishness for thee to kick against a goad." <div eID="gen44010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44011" type="x-p"/> Ovid has the same idea in other words, Trist. lib. ii. ver. 15: - <div eID="gen44011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44012" type="x-p"/> At nunc (tanta meo comes est insania morbo) <div eID="gen44012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44013" type="x-p"/> Saxa malum refero rursus ad icta pedem. <div eID="gen44013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44014" type="x-p"/> Scilicet et victus repetit gladiator arenam; <div eID="gen44014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44015" type="x-p"/> Et redit in tumidas naufraga puppis aquas. <div eID="gen44015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44016" type="x-p"/> But madly now I wound myself alone, <div eID="gen44016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44017" type="x-p"/> Dashing my injured foot against the stone: <div eID="gen44017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44018" type="x-p"/> So to the wide arena, wild with pain, <div eID="gen44018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44019" type="x-p"/> The vanquish'd gladiator hastes again; <div eID="gen44019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44020" type="x-p"/> So the poor shatter'd bark the tempest braves, <div eID="gen44020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44021" type="x-p"/> Launching once more into the swelling waves. <div eID="gen44021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44022" type="x-p"/> Intelligent men, in all countries and in all ages of the world, have seen and acknowledged the folly and wickedness of fighting against God; of murmuring at the dispensations of his providence; of being impatient under affliction; and of opposing the purposes of his justice and mercy. The words contain a universal lesson, and teach us patience under affliction, and subjection to the sovereign will of God; and they especially show the desperate wickedness of endeavoring, by persecution, to hinder the dissemination of the truth of God in the earth. He that kicks against this goad does it at the risk of his final salvation. The fable of the viper and the file is another illustration of this proverb: it gnawed and licked the file, till it destroyed its teeth and wasted away its tongue. The maxim in the proverb should be early inculcated on the minds of children and scholars; when chastised for their faults, resistance and stubbornness produce increased coercion and chastisement. And let parents and masters learn that the oft-repeated use of the goad and ferula seldom tend to reclaim, but beget obduracy and desperation. The advice of Columella to the ploughman, having some relation to the proverb in the text, and a strong bearing on this latter part of the subject, is worthy of the most serious regard: "Voce potius quam verberibus terreat: ultimaque sint opus recusantibus remedia plagae. Nunquam stimulo lacessat juvencum, quod retrectantem calcitrosumque eum reddit: nonnunquam tamen admoneat flagello." Columella, De Re Rustica, lib. ii. cap. 2, in fine. "Let the husbandman intimidate his oxen more by his voice than by blows, to which he should never have recourse but in extreme cases. A young steer should never be goaded, for this will induce him to kick and run back; but on proper occasions the whip, as an incentive to activity, may be profitably used." In reference to the same subject, which all concerned should feel to be of the greatest importance I shall close with the advice of one greater than the Roman agriculturist: Fathers, provoke not your children to anger, lest they be discouraged, <reference osisRef="Col.3.21">Col 3:21</reference>; but bring them up (εν παιδειᾳ και νουθεσιᾳ Κυριου) in the discipline and admonition of the Lord, <reference osisRef="Eph.6.4">Eph 6:4</reference>, using the authority that God has given you with a steady hand, actuated by a tender and feeling heart.
entries.1e2ec0700c606d59fb09092074304bdb1bf3df32: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen44022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44023" type="x-p"/> Trembling - Under a strong apprehension of meeting the judgment he deserved. <div eID="gen44023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44024" type="x-p"/> And astonished - At the light, the thunder, and the voice. <div eID="gen44024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44025" type="x-p"/> Lord, what wilt thou have me to do? - The word Κυριε, Lord, is here to be understood in its proper sense, as expressing authority and dominion: in the 5th verse it appears to be equivalent to our word sir. <div eID="gen44025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44026" type="x-p"/> The pride of the Pharisee is now brought down to the dust; and the fury of the persecutor is not only restrained, but the lion becomes a lamb. What wilt thou have me to do? Wilt thou condescend to employ me among thy meanest servants? <div eID="gen44026" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44027" type="x-p"/> Go into the city, and it shall be told thee, etc. - Jesus could have informed him at once what was his will concerning him; but he chose to make one of those very disciples whom he was going to bring in bonds to Jerusalem the means of his salvation: <div eID="gen44027" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44028" type="x-p"/> 1. To show that God will help man by man, that they may learn to love and respect each other. <div eID="gen44028" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44029" type="x-p"/> 2. That in the benevolence of Ananias he might see the spirit and tendency of that religion which he was persecuting, and of which he was shortly to become an apostle.
entries.4d7bc2d8526d73eefa3c9e7e6c0fe8d1531d4926: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen44029" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44030" type="x-p"/> Stood speechless, hearing a voice, but seeing no man - The men were εννεοι, stupified, hearing της φωνης, the voice or thunder, but not distinguishing the words, which were addressed to Saul alone; and which were spoken out of the thunder, or in a small, still voice, after the peal had ceased. The remarkable case, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.19.11-1Kgs.19.13">1Kgs 19:11-13</reference>, may serve to illustrate that before us. And he said, Go forth, and stand upon the mount before the Lord; and the Lord passed by, and a great and strong wind rent the mountains, and brake in pieces the rocks before the Lard; and after the wind an earthquake; and after the earthquake a fire; and after the fire a still small voice; and when Elijah heard it, he wrapped his face in his mantle, and went out, and stood in the entering in of the cave, and behold, there came a voice unto him, and said, What Dost Thou Here, Elijah! The thunder must have been heard by all; the small, still voice by Saul alone. This consideration amply reconciles the passage in the text with that in <reference osisRef="Act.22.9">Act 22:9</reference>, where Paul says, They that were with me saw the light and were afraid, but they heard not the voice of him that spoke with one. They had heard the thunder which followed the escape of the lightning, but they heard not the voice of him that spake to Saul; they did not hear the words, I am Jesus whom thou persecutest, etc.; but they saw and heard enough to convince them that the whole was supernatural; for they were all struck down to the earth with the splendor of the light, and the sound of the thunder, which I suppose took place on this occasion. It has been a question among divines, whether Jesus Christ did really appear to Saul on this occasion. The arguments against the real appearance are not strong. St. Luke tells us that those who were with him heard the voice, but they saw no man; which is a strong intimation that he saw what they did not. Ananias, it seems, was informed that there had been a real appearance, for, in addressing Saul, <reference osisRef="Act.9.17">Act 9:17</reference>, he says, The Lord Jesus that Appeared unto Thee in the way as thou camest, etc. And Barnabas intimates thus much, when he brought him before the apostles at Jerusalem, for he declared unto them how he had Seen the Lord in the way, and that he had spoken unto him; and, <reference osisRef="Act.22.14">Act 22:14</reference>, where the discourse of Ananias is given more at large, he says, The God of our fathers hath chosen thee that thou shouldest know his will, and See that Just One, and shouldest Hear the voice of his mouth; so we find that hearing the voice, or words of his mouth, was not what is called the appearance; for, besides this, there was an actual manifestation of the person of Christ. But St. Paul's own words, <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.1">1Cor 9:1</reference>, put the subject out of dispute: Am I not an apostle? Am I not free? Have I Not Seen Jesus Christ Our Lord? To which may be added, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.8">1Cor 15:8</reference>, And last of all, He Was Seen of Me Also, as of one born out of due time.
entries.b0c2d8f73895a3c0205699dab1442a1b29db1bda: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen44030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44031" type="x-p"/> When his eyes were opened, he saw no man - Instead of ουδενα, no man, the Codex Alexandrinus, the Syriac, Vulgate, and some others, have ουδεν nothing. He not only saw no man, but he saw nothing, being quite blind; and therefore was led by the hand to Damascus, μη βλεπων, being without sight.
entries.7c71198f45f41f700f1b5d4c9a2ddb4570433472: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen44031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44032" type="x-p"/> Neither did eat nor drink - The anxiety of his mind and the anguish of his heart were so great that he had no appetite for food; and he continued in total darkness and without food for three days, till Ananias proclaimed salvation to him in the name of the Lord Jesus.
entries.8958564364e98484bc1e1e60747188b059720b51: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen44032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44033" type="x-p"/> A certain disciple - named Ananias - A general opinion has prevailed in the Greek Church that this Ananias was one of the seventy-two disciples, and that he was martyred; and they celebrate his martyrdom on the first of October. It has been farther stated that his house was turned into a church, which remains to the present day, though now occupied as a Turkish mosque; but even the Mohammedans have the tradition, and treat his memory with great respect. However this may be, from <reference osisRef="Act.22.12">Act 22:12</reference>, we learn, what is of more importance, that he was a devout man according to the law, having a good report of all the Jews that dwelt there. See on <reference osisRef="Act.9.17">Act 9:17</reference> (note). <div eID="gen44033" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44034" type="x-p"/> To him said the Lord in a vision - Εν ὁραματι, In a strong impression made upon his mind, which left no doubt concerning its heavenly origin, nor of the truth of the things represented by it. It is very probable that the whole took place in a dream.
entries.7dd0fb52cf3a6004ce7bb7acefd57225d1e20430: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen44034" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44035" type="x-p"/> Arise, and go into the street which is called Straight - How very particular is this direction! And it was necessary that it should be so, that he might see the whole to be a Divine communication; the house was probably one in which Saul was accustomed to reside when at Damascus; and where he was known as a native of Tarsus. <div eID="gen44035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen44036" type="x-p"/> Tarsus was a city of Cilicia, seated on the Cydnus, and now called Tarasso. It was, at one period, the capital of all Cilicia, and became a rival to Alexandria and Athens in the arts and sciences.
